lead.headline: EU Leaders Leave Brussels With No Deal on the Next Seven-Year Budget
lead.deck: A 1.78 trillion euro compromise drew fire from every side, and the clock is set by 1 January 2028.
body: Money is the hardest subject at any EU summit. On Thursday 26 November the bloc’s leaders gathered in Brussels to end a deadlock over the next seven-year budget, the spending plan that is meant to run from 1 January 2028. They went home empty-handed: leaders would not move off their red lines, and some doubted that a deal was possible by December.

The draft they fought over was a compromise by Council President Costa, who chairs these summits. It totals 1.78 trillion euros in current prices over the seven years, which is 10% below the original draft, yet it drew pushback from all sides. Costa’s own message was that Europe cannot afford failure and needs a budget in place from the first day of 2028.

The sides want opposite things. Seven states called the Frugals demand deep cuts, while 17 Friends of Cohesion refuse further ones. Germany’s Friedrich Merz sided with the Frugals and said cuts would go beyond the 204 billion euros in Costa’s paper. The Frugals boycotted Costa’s small-group format, feeling singled out. Italy’s Giorgia Meloni judged a deal “light years away”; the Netherlands’ Rob Jetten saw “no need to hurry”.

One leader did set a deadline. France’s Emmanuel Macron demanded a deal by 31 December or he would walk away, and called the proposed cuts a “strategic mistake”; other states read this as a bargaining tactic. Meanwhile, leaders had settled Christine Lagarde’s succession at the European Central Bank before the talks, but a 45 billion euro loan for wartime Ukraine slipped down the agenda. Costa ended talks early, so Friday’s session was cancelled, and no date exists for the next round.

lead.why: The budget decides what the EU can spend from 2028 and how much each country pays in. With seven states demanding cuts and 17 opposing them, and a decision that needs every member on board, one holdout can stall the money for projects, regions and Ukraine.

world.headline: El Nino Is Heading for Record Strength, the World Weather Body Warns
world.deck: The WMO expects the Pacific warm spell to peak around December and to last into 2027.
body: Some of the year’s wildest weather starts as a patch of unusually warm water thousands of kilometres from most of the people it affects. That is El Nino, a warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that shifts rain, heat and drought around the world. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the UN’s weather agency, says El Nino has strengthened since August and is expected to reach record strength by December 2026, raising the risk of extreme weather into 2027.

Forecasters measure its strength with a number. The Nino 3.4 anomaly is how far the water temperature in a central strip of the tropical Pacific sits above its normal level. The WMO forecasts that the October to December average will be about 3.7 degrees Celsius above normal, peaking around December, and it sees a near-100 per cent likelihood that El Nino will persist through February 2027.

It arrives on a planet that is already running hot. For January to September 2026 the global mean near-surface temperature was 1.47 degrees Celsius (give or take 0.13) above the 1850-1900 average, and the four years from 2023 to 2026 are the four warmest on record. Global mean sea level reached its highest point in the satellite record, which began in 1993, and preliminary data through July point to a tenth consecutive year of record ocean heat content. The WMO update covers data to September, so it does not yet reflect El Nino’s most recent impacts.

Those impacts are already being reported. A France 24 roundup of 25 November described droughts in the Pacific and flooding in San Francisco, and noted that Oxford Economics estimates an intense El Nino could cut 0.6% of world GDP in 2027 and 0.8% in 2028. For India, the link is the monsoon: the government said El Nino conditions and a delayed monsoon, with rainfall deficits of 35 to 40 per cent in several regions, affected this year’s kharif sowing.

world.connect: Geography and economics: El Nino ties the Pacific to the Indian monsoon, so a warm ocean far away can shrink rainfall on Indian farms, the same shortfall that hit this year’s kharif sowing. Oxford Economics estimates the damage could reach 0.6% of world GDP in 2027.

india.headline: Finance Minister Wraps Up Pre-Budget Talks, Adding Young People for the First Time
india.deck: Thirteen meetings with more than 200 stakeholders feed into the Union Budget for 2027-28.
body: Before a government decides how to raise and spend money, it listens. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has now finished that listening for the Union Budget 2027-28, with pre-budget consultations that ran from 16 to 26 November 2026. The Union Budget is the government’s yearly statement of how it will raise money and where it will spend it.

The scale was wide. She chaired 13 meetings with more than 200 stakeholders drawn from 13 sectors and groups, so that the people who will feel the budget get to tell the government what they need from it. One thing was new this year: a consultation with young people, so that young voices were heard in the room for the first time.

The proposals that reached the table show how varied the asks are. Samples included domestic manufacturing of biofertilisers, sector-specific AI models, cyber-hygiene awareness for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and a reading movement so that every child can read a newspaper by the end of Grade 5. Some of these would cost public money and some mostly need policy changes, which is the trade-off the finance ministry must weigh.

A consultation is not a promise. The suggestions are inputs, and the final package is decided by the government and presented to Parliament. The article does not say when the Union Budget 2027-28 will be presented, so the date is still to be announced.

The process follows a set pattern. The government places an annual financial statement, the Union Budget, before Parliament, and the Finance Minister presents it. The 2027-28 financial year starts on 1 April 2027, so the government needs its spending plan ready by then. In recent years it has been presented on 1 February. Stakeholders, in this context, means groups with a stake in the outcome: industry bodies, farmers, economists and, this year, young people. Hearing them first does not bind the government, but it shows it which problems are loudest.

Each sample proposal shows a different kind of ask. Biofertilisers are fertilisers made from living microorganisms, so making them at home would be a farm and industry policy. Cyber-hygiene awareness means teaching small firms basic habits such as strong passwords and safe online payments. A budget has two halves, the money the government expects to receive, mainly from taxes, and the money it plans to spend, and every new scheme has to fit within them.

india.why: The budget sets how the government raises and spends money, so the pre-budget talks are where farmers, industry and now young people can shape what gets funded. Proposals are only suggestions until the government decides.

politics_and_civics.headline: A Regional Health Body Rules the US Has Lost Its Measles Elimination Status
politics_and_civics.deck: The Pan American Health Organization says the virus is again spreading for good in the US, Mexico and Bolivia, and the US must file a plan to win the status back.
body: A country can lose a health title the way a team loses a league place, and on 17 November 2026 the United States did. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s regional office for the Americas, announced that endemic measles transmission has been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, so all three lost their measles elimination status. A disease is called endemic when it keeps circulating in a place on its own.

The test is strict and technical. Endemic transmission is considered re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulates uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country. In the US that has been met: the country is reporting more than 5,400 cases and 10 associated deaths. Even the death toll is disputed between layers of government, because states report 13 deaths while the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recognizes nine.

The US government’s answer is to separate the label from the protection. The CDC says losing the status does not mean measles is widespread in every community; risk is concentrated where vaccination is lower. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said: “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.” The numbers behind that point are close to the problem: about 92 percent of US kindergarteners got the measles vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019, and about 95% is needed to block spread.

The path back is set out too. The US can regain elimination status if measles spread is stopped for at least 12 consecutive months, and it must submit a plan for how to do it. That puts the next move with Washington and the states, since vaccination levels are decided through public policy and individual choices rather than by the international body that announced the ruling.

The stakes are practical. Measles spreads through the air, and one infected person can pass it to as many as 12 to 18 unvaccinated people, which is why the vaccination level matters more than the label. In the US, states set the school vaccination rules, so the recovery plan will depend on 50 state governments as much as on Washington. The health body’s ruling therefore works as a public report card: it does not punish anyone, but it records that a goal once met has slipped.

illustration.title: WHO DECIDES, WHO ACTS
illustration.subtitle: 17 November 2026
illustration.caption: PAHO announced the loss of status for three countries; vaccination policy stays with national and state governments.

politics_and_civics.why: An international body can name a problem, but only national and state governments can fix it, through vaccination policy and public persuasion. The ruling shows how health rules, official counts and public trust meet in civic life.

economics.headline: Public Sector Banks Lend 127 Lakh Crore Rupees as Bad Loans Fall to a Record Low
economics.deck: Net bad loans stand at 0.33% of lending, while credit to farmers and small firms is growing faster than retail loans.
body: When banks are healthy, households and firms can borrow more cheaply, so the state of the banks matters well beyond finance. Government data show that as of 30 September 2026, public sector banks’ gross advances, meaning the total loans they have given out, were 127 lakh crore rupees, up 18.8% year on year. Total deposits, the savings customers keep with the banks, were 165.2 lakh crore rupees, up 12.9%.

The loans are also getting safer. A net non-performing asset (NPA) is a loan whose repayments have stalled, after the bank has set aside money to cover the loss. Net NPAs were 44,100 crore rupees, or 0.33% of total advances, described as a historic low. New trouble is shrinking as well: slippages, the loans that newly turn bad, fell from 1.44 lakh crore rupees in the 2021-22 financial year to 38,780 crore in the first half of 2026-27.

Who is getting the credit? Year-on-year growth in lending was 17% for retail borrowers, 19.5% for agriculture and 20.4% for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), the small firms that employ many people. Among individual banks, Bank of Maharashtra recorded the highest credit growth. The chart sets these growth rates side by side, with the overall figure for comparison.

Two caveats keep the picture honest. These are figures released by the government, and growth in lending is not the same as growth in the real economy: a loan only helps if it is repaid. A low bad-loan ratio shows banks are collecting repayments today, not that every future loan will be safe.

A note on the numbers helps. One lakh crore rupees is a trillion rupees, so the 127 lakh crore of advances is a very large sum. Lending grew faster than deposits, 18.8% against 12.9%, which means banks are lending out savings quickly. That is good for borrowers while it lasts, but banks need steady deposits to keep funding new loans, so the gap is worth watching in future releases.

economics.why: Banks turn savings into loans for farms, shops and homes. With fewer bad loans, they can lend more, but only if borrowers keep repaying.
economics.analyst: Credit to agriculture and MSMEs is growing faster than retail lending. What could explain that gap, and what would you need to know about repayment to judge whether faster growth is healthy? If net bad loans are at a historic low, does that make lending riskier or safer from here?

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth, and Engineers Keep Switching Things Off to Save It
science_and_technology.deck: The probe is about 25.9 billion kilometres away, and its power supply is slowly fading.
body: A signal sent to Voyager 1 now takes a full day to arrive. On 18 November 2026, at 2:16:07 a.m. PST, NASA’s probe passed one light-day from Earth, the distance light travels in a day. It was 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion kilometres) away. It is the first spacecraft to get so far, though NASA says the probe will not detect any change in its environment as it passes the mark, and nothing changes aboard.

The milestone sits beside a quieter problem. Voyager 1 runs on a radioisotope power generator, which turns heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. With the plutonium supply depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. To keep the spacecraft operating, engineers have had to give up instruments one by one.

The latest sacrifice came in April 2026, when engineers sent commands to shut down the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment (LECP). NASA’s status table lists the Cosmic Ray Subsystem as off to save power since 25 February 2025, and the cameras were turned off in 1990. As of the April 2026 report, two science instruments were still working on Voyager 1: one that listens to plasma waves and one that measures magnetic fields.

Each shutdown is a trade between science and survival. Keeping every instrument on would end the mission sooner; turning them off gives the remaining ones more time to report from interstellar space, the region beyond the Sun’s planets. NASA’s own mission page and blog describe the choices, which is why the probe’s length of service depends less on distance than on how many watts remain.

The scale is hard to picture, so compare it with light from the Sun, which takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. Voyager 1 is still sending data across that gap. Its cameras went dark in 1990, after taking pictures of the Solar System. Today its voice is faint: commands take a day to reach it, and its answers take a day to return, so every instruction must be planned carefully.

What the two working instruments do is also worth knowing. A plasma wave instrument picks up the vibrations of electrically charged gas around the probe, and a magnetometer measures the strength and direction of magnetic fields. Together they let scientists read conditions in a region no other spacecraft has reached. Voyager 1 also flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, which is why it is remembered as one of the great planetary explorers.

explainer.title: How the EU agrees a seven-year budget
body: The European Union does not pass its spending plans year by year. Every few years it sets a long-term budget, which this time covers seven years starting on 1 January 2028. The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, proposes the first draft. The leaders of the member states, meeting as the European Council, then bargain over the size of the budget, who pays in and what it is spent on.

The key rule is unanimity: the member states in the Council of the EU must all agree to adopt the long-term budget, and the European Parliament must also give its consent. That means one country can block a deal, which is why leaders hold “red lines” and why camps form. In this round the Frugals want deep cuts and the Friends of Cohesion oppose them; cohesion money is spent to help less wealthy regions catch up with richer ones. For an exam answer, remember the pattern: proposal, bargaining among governments, unanimous agreement, then parliamentary consent.

lead.headline: EU Leaders Cannot Agree on Their Money Plan
body: The European Union is a group of countries that work together. Its leaders met in Brussels on Thursday 26 November. They wanted to agree how much money the group will have for seven years.
They did not agree. A leader named Costa offered a plan worth 1.78 trillion euros. That was 10% less than the first plan. Even so, every side said no.

Seven countries want deep cuts. Seventeen countries want no more cuts. The new budget should start on 1 January 2028. France’s Macron said there must be a deal by 31 December. Nobody knows when they will meet again.

world.headline: A Warm Patch of Ocean May Cause Wild Weather
body: El Nino is a warming of the water in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It can change rain and heat all over the world.
The World Meteorological Organization says El Nino is getting stronger. It expects a record by December. It says El Nino will almost surely last until February 2027.

Scientists track it with a number. This time the water is forecast to be about 3.7 degrees Celsius warmer than normal. The weather group also says sea levels have reached their highest point in satellite records.

india.headline: India’s Finance Minister Asks Many People for Ideas
body: Every year India’s government makes a money plan called the Union Budget. Before that, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman listens to people.
From 16 to 26 November she held 13 meetings. More than 200 people from 13 sectors and groups took part. For the first time, young people were asked too.
Some ideas were new. One was a reading movement so every child can read a newspaper by the end of Grade 5. The government will decide what to use.

politics_and_civics.headline: The US Loses Its Measles-Free Title
body: Measles is an illness that spreads very easily. A health group for the Americas said on 17 November that the United States has lost its measles-free status. Mexico and Bolivia lost it too.
The reason is that the same measles virus kept spreading for 12 months or more. The US has more than 5,400 cases.
Doctors say about 95% of people need the vaccine to stop spread. In 2025 about 92 percent of US kindergarteners got it. The US can win the title back if spread stops for 12 months in a row.

economics.headline: Indian Banks Lend More and Have Fewer Bad Loans
body: Banks lend out the money that people save. A bad loan is one that the borrower has stopped paying back.
The government says public sector banks had given out 127 lakh crore rupees in loans by 30 September 2026. That is 18.8% more than a year earlier.
Bad loans have fallen to just 0.33% of all loans. Loans to farmers grew 19.5%, and loans to small firms grew 20.4%.

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1 Is One Light-Day Away
body: A light-day is how far light travels in one whole day. On 18 November 2026 NASA’s Voyager 1 reached that distance from Earth. It is 25.902 billion kilometres away.
The probe gets power from a plutonium generator. Each year it loses about 4 watts of power. To save power, engineers turn off instruments.
In April 2026 they shut off one more. Only two science instruments are still working. They listen to waves and measure magnetic fields.
